name: Issue Tracker
description: A tiny issue tracker for a small software team with tickets, comments, status changes, audit history, and role-based permissions.

turns.question: What is the primary goal of this issue tracker? Are you looking to replace an existing tool, or is this a new workflow for the team?
turns.why: Understanding whether this replaces an existing process helps scope the migration effort and identify must-have features vs nice-to-haves.
turns.answer: Replace our spreadsheet — we need proper tracking from creation to completion

options.content: Replace an existing tool (e.g., spreadsheet, email threads) with a purpose-built tracker
Introduce issue tracking as a new practice — the team currently has no formal process
Supplement an existing enterprise tool (e.g., Jira) with a lighter alternative for smaller projects

turns.freeText: We're currently using a shared Google Sheet and it's painful — no history, no accountability

turns.question: Who are the primary users of this system, and how large is the team?
turns.why: Team size and user roles directly influence the permission model, notification complexity, and performance requirements.
turns.answer: About 8 developers across 2-3 projects, plus a couple of managers who need visibility

options.content: A small team (under 10 people) working on 1-3 projects
A medium team (10-30 people) with multiple squads and project leads
A cross-functional group including developers, QA, product managers, and stakeholders

turns.freeText: About 8 developers across 2-3 projects, plus a couple of managers who want read-only dashboards

turns.question: What are the key entities the system needs to track? Think about the core objects users will create and interact with daily.
turns.why: Defining the entity model early prevents scope creep — each entity adds CRUD, permissions, and relationship complexity.
turns.answer: Tickets with status, assignee, priority — plus comments for discussion and audit

options.content: Tickets (work items) with status, assignee, priority, and description
Tickets plus epics or parent groupings for organizing related work
Tickets, sprints, and a backlog with capacity planning

turns.freeText: Each ticket should also support comments — timestamped notes for discussion and status updates

turns.question: Are there compliance or audit requirements for this system? Some teams need to prove who changed what and when.
turns.why: Audit trail requirements affect the data model significantly — they may require immutable event logs rather than simple CRUD updates.
turns.answer: Yes, we need full audit history for compliance — every status change must be traceable

options.content: Full audit trail required — every status change must record who, what, and when
Basic change history is nice to have but not a compliance requirement
No audit requirements — simple current-state tracking is sufficient

turns.question: What constraints should we establish for the v1 scope? Understanding what you explicitly want to exclude helps keep the first version focused.
turns.why: Explicit constraints prevent scope creep and help prioritize — knowing what's out helps clarify what's in.
turns.answer: Keep it simpler than Jira, add role-based permissions with three roles

options.content: Keep it deliberately simpler than Jira — no custom workflows, no custom fields in v1
Match Jira's core feature set but with a cleaner UX
Build a minimal viable tracker and expand based on user feedback

turns.freeText: We need role-based permissions though — admin, developer, and viewer roles

turns.answer: Scope context is well-defined: the team needs a simple issue tracker replacing their spreadsheet, with tickets, comments, audit history, and role-based permissions for ~8 developers.
Confirm grounding closure

turns.question: How should the primary interface be organized? The team needs to see ticket status at a glance — what layout best supports that?
turns.why: The primary view determines the mental model users build around the tool. A board-style layout emphasizes flow; a list-style layout emphasizes filtering and bulk operations.
turns.answer: Kanban board with swimlanes per assignee — that's how we think about work

options.content: Kanban board with columns per status and optional swimlanes per assignee
Sortable table view with inline editing and bulk actions
Combined view with a board as default and table as an alternative

turns.question: How should the audit trail be implemented? This affects both data model complexity and query performance.
turns.why: The audit implementation is a core architectural decision — an event-sourced log is more complete but harder to query, while comment-based logging is simpler but may miss some changes.
turns.answer: Comment-based activity log — simpler and keeps everything in one timeline per ticket

options.content: Comment-based activity log — status changes appear as system-generated comments in the ticket timeline
Separate audit table with structured event records for each field change
Event-sourced model where the ticket state is derived from an append-only event log

turns.freeText: This also means the comment timeline becomes the single source of truth for what happened on a ticket
